faqs.answer: An eclipsing binary is a pair of stars orbiting around their common center of mass. From Earth, we see their orbital plane edge-on (or nearly so), meaning one star periodically passes in front of the other. When it does, the total light we receive from the system dips. By observing these dips, we can measure the orbital period and the relative sizes and brightnesses of the two stars.
faqs.question: What is an eclipsing binary?

faqs.answer: A 'candidate' is a star whose light curve shows a periodic brightness dip consistent with an eclipsing binary. A 'confirmed' candidate is one that has passed Star Vetter's automated pixel-level check - meaning the dip comes from the target star itself, not from contamination by a nearby background star. 'Confirmed' is a technical term for this project's vetting stage, not a claim of independent scientific verification.
faqs.question: What does 'candidate' mean here, and how is it different from 'confirmed'?

faqs.answer: Star Vetter trains a machine-learning model (hist_gradient_boosting) on examples it has already pixel-checked. This model learns to rank candidates by their likelihood of passing that check. It provides a second opinion on our rule-based pipeline and outperforms the baseline in ranking quality. However, it does not gate which candidates get checked - every candidate that passes our statistical tests and novelty cross-match goes to pixel-level inspection regardless of the ML score.
faqs.question: What is the machine-learning screening score?

faqs.answer: The pixel-level check is an automated test that examines whether the eclipse signal comes from the target star's pixels or from nearby background stars. It runs on the full-frame image data from TESS to rule out false positives caused by blended light from nearby objects. This check is performed entirely by algorithm, with no manual review.
faqs.question: How does the pixel-level check work?

faqs.answer: The period alias check compares the brightness dips from odd-numbered eclipses against those from even-numbered eclipses. If the two are significantly different, it may indicate that the measured period is an alias - twice the true orbital period, for example. Candidates flagged by this test carry a caveat on their individual pages noting the ambiguity.
faqs.question: What does the period alias check do?

faqs.answer: Yes. Each candidate page includes a link to the TESS light-curve data in the Mikulski Archive for Space Telescopes (MAST). You can download the data and inspect the periodogram and light curve yourself. We encourage independent assessment - our vetting is a starting point, not a final word.
faqs.question: Can I verify a confirmed candidate myself?

faqs.answer: Being listed here marks the end of what this automated pipeline does. We do not perform follow-up observation, obtain radial-velocity measurements, publish results, or add candidates to official catalogs. Each confirmed candidate is a signal worth investigating further - but what happens next is up to the broader astronomy community.
faqs.question: What happens to a candidate after it is listed on Star Vetter?

narrative: Star Vetter automatically identifies eclipsing binary stars in data from NASA's TESS satellite. An eclipsing binary is a pair of stars orbiting each other, periodically passing in front of each other from Earth's perspective and dimming the light we receive. TESS observes hundreds of thousands of stars; Star Vetter applies statistical tests to their light curves, checks whether candidates are already known, and runs an automated pixel-level check to confirm that the dip in brightness comes from the target star itself rather than a nearby background object. Each candidate listed here has passed those checks. We cross-reference six major variable-star catalogs to avoid re-listing known systems, and we train a machine-learning model on our checked examples so we can compare its ranking against our standard pipeline. The result is a catalog of candidates ready for follow-up study - not a claim that every system is scientifically confirmed, but a curated collection of strong signals worth investigating further.
